ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Ella Fitzgerald Synthetic CCD — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: New patient visit: diabetes with calf pain on walking, low glucose after late shows, eye and foot examinations, and cardiovascular risk. Concerns: Her calves cramp when she walks through airports and to the stage, and she is afraid of what that means for her legs; Her glucose has dropped low after late shows, once just before an encore; The vision in her right eye has blurred, and she worries about reading lyrics and set lists. [S]

list.item: Type 2 diabetes mellitus with peripheral artery disease: cramping in both calves after about one and a half blocks of walking, worse on the right, easing within minutes of rest; no rest pain, wounds, or color change. Resting ankle-brachial index 0.62 right and 0.74 left, toe-brachial index 0.46 and 0.55; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses absent on the right and faint on the left. A1c 8.6% on metformin, glipizide and glargine, with low glucose readings (to 52 mg/dL) after late performances. Foot: protective sensation intact to the 10-g monofilament at all sites and to vibration; callus under the second metatarsal heads; hammer toes of the second and third toes; no ulcer (IWGDF risk category 2). Synthetic modern episode linked to her documented diabetes and its circulatory complications: active, confirmed [S]

Moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy with center-involving diabetic macular edema in the right eye (best-corrected acuity 64 letters, about 20/50) and moderate nonproliferative retinopathy without macular edema in the left eye (81 letters); lens implants in both eyes from earlier cataract surgery. Synthetic modern episode linked to her documented diabetic eye problems: active, confirmed [S]

Coronary artery disease after five-vessel coronary bypass surgery last year, with an intensive care stay; no angina now; on aspirin, a statin, and metoprolol. Synthetic modern episode linked to her documented heart surgery: active, confirmed [S]

list.item: Singer; back on stage since recovering from her heart surgery, touring in the United States and overseas, often two or three late shows a week with long travel days and meals at irregular times; performing is the center of her life [S]
Lives in her own home; a road manager and her musicians travel with her; a long-time dresser helps her prepare for shows. She decides who is told about her health [S]
Tobacco: does not smoke. Alcohol: rarely (AUDIT-C at the wellness visit). No other drugs [S]
Activity: stands for long sets on stage in heeled shoes; walks little off stage because of calf pain [S]

Access and equity: Medicare with a Part D plan and a supplemental plan; misses appointments when touring; reads standard print with difficulty because of her right eye. The clinic schedules around tour dates, uses video visits on the road, sends large-print instructions, checks drug costs before prescribing, and coordinates with clinics in tour cities [S]
Supports and strengths: her music, her audiences, her band and road manager, and decades of experience of her own body on the road [S]

tr.td: New patient visit: diabetes with calf pain on walking, low glucose after late shows, eye and foot examinations, and cardiovascular risk
Two-week review: glucose and hypoglycemia safety on the new plan, and vascular surgery consultation
Three-month review: A1c, lipids, walking program, eye treatment, and foot care
Five-and-a-half-month review: A1c, lipids, walking distance, revascularization decision, foot and eye follow-up

Comprehensive diabetic foot program: foot inspection, monofilament and vibration testing, and pulses at every visit; IWGDF risk category 2 with podiatry every three months for callus and nail care; protective daily shoes and low-heeled custom stage shoes; daily self-inspection with a magnifying mirror or her dresser's help; and same-day care for any blister, wound, or color change

Vascular surgery consultation for claudication with an ankle-brachial index of 0.62: arterial duplex, supervised exercise therapy, and whether and when revascularization should be considered, before any loss of tissue

Hypoglycemia safety on tour: glipizide stopped; glargine reduced 20% and moved to the morning, at a fixed clock time with written time-zone steps; a continuous glucose monitor with low alerts shared, with her consent, with her road manager; a glucose check before each show and a meal before late shows; glucose tablets in the dressing room and at the side of the stage; nasal glucagon with the road manager trained; and the beta-blocker's effect on warning signs explained

Glucose-lowering medicines with heart and kidney benefit: empagliflozin 10 mg started, with sick-day rules (hold on days she cannot eat or drink and before surgery), genital hygiene advice, and a foot check at each visit; metformin continued with vitamin B12 checked; A1c every three months until at goal (goal below 7.5%)
Cardiovascular protection: atorvastatin raised to 80 mg with a lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks later and a goal LDL below 55 mg/dL; aspirin and metoprolol continued; blood pressure goal below 130/80 mmHg

Eye care: retina clinic appointment within two weeks for the right macular edema, for anti-VEGF injections; retinal examination of both eyes at least yearly and more often while being treated; large-print materials

Kidney and laboratory monitoring: creatinine, eGFR and potassium at three months and then every six to twelve months, urine albumin-creatinine ratio yearly, liver tests after the statin change if symptoms, and vitamin B12 periodically on metformin

Access and equity: scheduling around tour dates, video visits on the road, large-print instructions, drug-cost checks before prescribing, coordination with clinics in tour cities, and diabetes self-management education and medical nutrition therapy timed to her touring

Supervised exercise therapy for claudication: treadmill walking to moderate calf pain, 30 to 45 minutes three times a week for twelve weeks at a hospital program, with a structured home walking plan for tour weeks; then walking at least three times a week for life
Low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily with aspirin 81 mg to lower the risk of heart attack, stroke, and major limb events, with bleeding precautions and no anti-inflammatory painkillers

Revascularization plan: no procedure now; endovascular treatment of the right superficial femoral artery to be considered if claudication still limits her life after twelve weeks of supervised exercise and medical therapy; urgent vascular review for rest pain, a wound, or color change; ankle-brachial index and duplex at six months

Semaglutide 0.25 mg weekly for four weeks, then 0.5 mg weekly, for cardiovascular benefit and walking distance, with the retina clinic told before the start because a fast fall in glucose can briefly worsen retinopathy; ezetimibe 10 mg added for an LDL of 64 mg/dL
